title: It's 10pm. Do You Know Where Your Agents Are? — Kim Maida, Keycard

summary:
The talk opens with a nostalgic reference to 1960s–80s public service announcements asking parents whether they know where their children are. Maida draws a parallel to AI agents entrusted with increasing responsibility but often running unsupervised with broad API keys. A demo shows an incident management agent on the night shift triaging tickets—a backup power failure, an expiring TLS certificate, a broken billing database, frozen processes, and failing sites—using one kitchen-sink API key. When the documented fix says to drop the database and restore from backup, the agent drops the production Postgres database, cannot verify a backup ran, and escalates for the morning. This has happened to real companies.

Maida identifies three problems: credentials aren't attributed to user or agent identity, agents have unrestricted access to all permissions in an API key, and human-in-the-loop is insufficient because humans are consent-fatigued, tired, or absent. She traces the agentic execution path: user → runtime (CLI/SDK/app) → model → MCP client → MCP server → resource API, with results flowing back.

The fix is RFC 8693 (OAuth Token Exchange). The user authenticates and consents to delegate a subset of permissions. For each tool call, the OAuth client authenticates with a security token service using workload identity, sends the subject token with the user's identity and access level, and requests a token scoped to just that call's target MCP server. Governance policy evaluates the delegation chain and requested access. If within policy, the STS issues a short-lived, ephemeral, audience-restricted token, never stored, discarded after use.

A second demo shows the agent with token exchange enabled. The operator signs in via Google; the audit log shows who the agent acts on behalf of. Certificate renewal requests narrow scope. When the agent tries to drop the billing database, policy evaluates before the credential is minted, finds a restriction, and the credential never exists. When the agent wants to restart prod, the operator approves, but policy blocks it because the user lacks the required role—consent fatigue can't override policy. For scaling, the operator has permission, so approval proceeds.

Maida emphasizes open standards enable broad compatibility: works with off-the-shelf and custom agents, CLI, third-party and proprietary MCP servers, MCP gateways, agent-to-agent, and any OAuth provider. In Q&A, she clarifies the authorization server sits between the runtime and MCP server, evaluating requested scopes before issuing tokens. The spec isn't new—new specs can combine with token exchange. For teams starting scope definition, begin with the resource server's existing scopes as baseline, then layer tool-call scopes on top or pass them through.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Agents with long-lived kitchen-sink API keys are dangerously overprivileged—they can drop production databases, take production offline, and incur unplanned spending, even under human supervision.
Human-in-the-loop approval alone is insufficient: operators can be tired, consent-fatigued, or absent, and many agents run autonomously.
RFC 8693 (OAuth Token Exchange) enables per-tool-call token minting: each call gets a fresh, short-lived, audience-scoped token that is never stored.
Policy evaluation happens before a credential is minted—if the action is denied, the credential never exists, leaving nothing to leak, replay, or steal.
Human approval gains real teeth: even if an operator clicks approve, policy can block actions they lack the required role for, preventing consent fatigue from enabling dangerous operations.
Token exchange establishes an identity chain: the agent's identity, the user's identity, and the user's delegated access level are all known at decision time.
The approach works across CLI coding agents, MCP servers, SDKs, and any OAuth provider, using open standards rather than proprietary solutions.
For teams defining OAuth scopes, start with the resource server's existing scopes as a baseline, then layer tool-call-specific scopes on top or pass them through.

sections.title: Introduction: The 10pm Problem
sections.summary: Maida opens with a nostalgic reference to public service announcements from the 60s–80s asking parents if they know where their children are. She draws a parallel to AI agents being entrusted with increasing responsibility while running with broad API keys, often unsupervised.

sections.title: Demo: Incident Agent on the Night Shift
sections.summary: A live demo shows an incident management agent triaging night-shift tickets using a single kitchen-sink API key. It escalates a hardware failure, renews a TLS certificate, drops the production Postgres database per documented fix without verifying backups, takes prod offline for frozen processes, and scales up infrastructure—all with the same overprivileged key.

sections.title: Why Agents Are Dangerously Overprivileged
sections.summary: Maida explains that agents with API keys are overprivileged and act freely on decisions users may disagree with, even under supervision. Human-in-the-loop is insufficient because humans are consent-fatigued, tired, or absent, and many agents run autonomously.

sections.title: The Agentic Execution Path
sections.summary: Maida traces the full execution path: user submits a prompt to a runtime (CLI, SDK, or app), which calls the model; the model proposes tool calls dispatched by the MCP client to the MCP server, which calls the resource API; results flow back through the loop until the model returns a final answer.

sections.title: The Fix: OAuth Token Exchange (RFC 8693)
sections.summary: Maida introduces RFC 8693 (token exchange) as the solution. She recaps the three problems: unattributed credentials, unrestricted access, and insufficient human-in-the-loop. An authorization server (security token service) verifies identities and issues tokens after user consent to delegate a subset of their permissions—the first narrowing of access.

sections.title: Token Exchange Flow and Policy Evaluation
sections.summary: The OAuth client authenticates with the STS using workload identity and sends the subject token containing the user's identity and access level. For each tool call it requests a token scoped to just that action. Governance policy evaluates the delegation chain and requested access. If within policy, the STS issues a short-lived, ephemeral, audience-restricted token that is never stored and discarded after use.

sections.title: Demo Revisited with Token Exchange
sections.summary: The same agent runs with token exchange enabled. The operator signs in via Google. The audit log now shows who the agent acts on behalf of, which MCP server it calls, and downstream resources. Certificate renewal requests only a narrow scope. When the agent tries to drop the billing database, policy evaluates before the credential is minted, finds a restriction preventing agents from dropping databases, and the credential never exists—nothing to leak, replay, or steal.

sections.title: Human Approval Backed by Real Policy
sections.summary: The demo continues with two more scenarios. When the agent wants to restart prod, it asks for human approval; the operator approves, but policy blocks the action because the user lacks the required role—preventing consent fatigue from enabling dangerous actions. For infrastructure scaling, the operator has permission, so approval proceeds and policy allows it. Maida summarizes that all three core problems now have solutions: identity is known for both user and agent, access is task-scoped and short-lived, and human-in-the-loop is backed by real policy so an exhausted person can't just accept everything.

sections.title: Open Standards and Broad Compatibility
sections.summary: Maida emphasizes that using open standards like token exchange enables support for emerging technologies. The approach works with off-the-shelf and custom agents, CLI coding agents, third-party and proprietary MCP servers, MCP gateways, agent-to-agent communication, any OAuth identity provider, and future tools. She closes by introducing herself as founding GTM engineer and head of DevRel at Keycard, a standards-based platform for STS and policy governance, and announces a workshop on building and securing an MCP server.

sections.title: Q&A and Closing
sections.summary: In Q&A, Maida clarifies that the authorization server sits between the runtime and the MCP server: the runtime authenticates to the STS, which evaluates the agent's requested scopes before issuing a downstream token, ensuring the agent only receives tokens within approved scope. She addresses enterprise adoption concerns by noting the spec is not new—RFC 8693 has existed for some time—and new specs can be combined with token exchange. For teams starting scope definition, she recommends beginning with the resource server's existing scopes as a baseline, then layering additional tool-call scopes on top or passing them through.
